hints: Compare what you observe when each compound is mixed with cold water, one reacts vigorously and one shows no reaction under normal conditions.
Think about the environment of the C-Cl bond in each case, what the chlorine lone pair can interact with in chlorobenzene and what electron withdrawing groups surround carbon in ethanoyl chloride.
walkthrough:
Picture the two C-Cl environments**
Do not treat both chlorides as the same. In $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ the $\text{Cl}$ is attached to a highly polar $\text{C=O}$ carbon. In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ the $\text{Cl}$ is attached directly to the benzene ring. That difference in bonding controls everything.

Why chlorobenzene is so inert**
Imagine the p orbital on $\text{Cl}$ holding a lone pair sitting side on to the pi system of the ring. The lone pair can delocalise into the ring. This overlap gives the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character, it becomes shorter and stronger, so water cannot break it under normal conditions.

Why ethanoyl chloride is so reactive**
Now look at $\text{CH}_3\text{-C(=O)-Cl}$. Oxygen is very electronegative and pulls electrons away from carbon, chlorine does the same. The carbonyl carbon is therefore very $\delta+$, very electron deficient. Water as a nucleophile attacks it very easily, and the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks readily to give $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{HCl}$.

Final answer: Ethanoyl chloride reacts vigorously with water, chlorobenzene does not react.
In chlorobenzene the chlorine lone pair overlaps and delocalises into the benzene ring, giving the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character and strengthening it. In ethanoyl chloride the carbonyl carbon is very electron deficient due to two electronegative atoms ($\text{O}$ and $\text{Cl}$) and the $\text{C=O}$ group, so it is readily attacked and the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is weakened.

hints: Scan structure V from left to right and label each carbon attached to N or O, remembering that $\text{-CN}$, $\text{-CONH-}$, $\text{-CO-}$ and $\text{-COO-}$ look similar but have different connectivities.
Check the right hand ring carefully, one oxygen is inside the ring and joined to $\text{C=O}$, which is characteristic of a cyclic ester rather than a simple ether or ketone.
walkthrough:
Work left to right through V**
On the cyclohexane ring you see $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$, that is a nitrile. Next to it $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ linking to $\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$, that is an amide.

Spot the two carbonyls on the right**
In the middle $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-CH-}$ where carbon is joined only to carbons, that is a ketone. On the far right the five membered ring has $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ joined in a ring, that is an ester, specifically a lactone.
Final answer: nitrile ($\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$), amide ($\text{-CONH-}$), ketone ($\text{-CO-}$) / carbonyl, ester ($\text{-COO-}$ / lactone)

hints: Count carbon atoms bonded to four different groups in V, look at the two substituted carbons on the cyclohexane ring and the carbon where the lactone oxygen attaches.
walkthrough:
Count chiral centres then use powers of two**
Find carbons with four different groups. There are two on the disubstituted cyclohexane ring and one at the $\text{O-CH-}$ position next to the ketone. That is 3 chiral centres in total, so number of stereoisomers $= 2^3 = 8$.
Final answer: 8 optical isomers (3 chiral centres, $2^3 = 8$)

hints: Think about what extra practical step is needed if you make a mixture of optical isomers but only one is wanted as a drug.
walkthrough:
Why make one isomer directly**
If you synthesise the mixture you must then separate the active isomer from the inactive isomers, which is difficult and expensive. Making only the desired isomer avoids that separation step. It also avoids the risk that another isomer has no effect or harmful side effects.
Final answer: No need to separate optical isomers, saving time and cost / avoids possible harmful side effects of the unwanted isomer.

hints: List which groups in V hydrolyse in hot aqueous alkali and which survive, remember nitrile, amide and ester all hydrolyse but ketone does not.
Remember at pH 12 all carboxylic acids exist as $\text{COO}^{-}$ and amines exist as free $\text{NH}_2$, not $\text{NH}_3^{+}$.

Split V at the amide link to give two fragments, the left cyclohexane fragment will gain two $\text{COO}^{-}$ groups and the right fragment will contain $\text{NH}_2$, ketone, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COO}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Decide what breaks and what stays**
Sit with V and mark it up. Hot $\text{NaOH}$ hydrolyses three types here: $\text{-CN}$, $\text{-CONH-}$ and lactone $\text{-COO-}$. The ketone $\text{-CO-}$ in the middle is untouched. The amide bond is the cut point that divides the molecule into two organic pieces.

Build the left hand product**
The cyclohexane has $\text{-CN}$ on one carbon and $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ on the adjacent carbon. Alkaline hydrolysis converts $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-COO}^{-}$ and converts the amide carbonyl to $\text{-COO}^{-}$. So you get a cyclohexane ring with two adjacent $\text{-COO}^{-}$ groups, the dicarboxylate dianion.

Build the right hand product**
The $\text{-NH-}$ side of the amide becomes $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-}$. The ketone $\text{-C(=O)-}$ stays as $\text{C=O}$. The lactone opens: $$ \text{-C(=O)-O-CH-} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{-COO}^{-} + \text{-CH(OH)-} $$ So the chain is $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-COO}^{-}$. At pH 12 carboxylates stay deprotonated and the amine stays as $\text{NH}_2$.

Final answer: Left product: cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylate dianion, ring with two adjacent $\text{COO}^{-}$ groups (from nitrile hydrolysis and amide $\text{C=O}$ hydrolysis).
Right product: $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-CH(OH)-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-COO}^{-}$ (from amide $\text{NH}$ hydrolysis to $\text{NH}_2$, ketone unchanged, lactone ester hydrolysis to $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COO}^{-}$).

hints: Recall that peak area is proportional to mass, so add all four peak areas to get the total mass measure before finding the share for A.
walkthrough:
Turn areas into a percentage**
Total area $= 28 + 58 + 13 + 42 = 141$. The share for A is: $$ \text{percentage} = 100 \times \frac{28}{141} = 19.9\% $$ Give at least 2 significant figures with a $\%$ sign.

hints: Remember that in GLC a longer retention time means the component spends more time dissolved in the stationary phase rather than moving with the carrier gas.
walkthrough:
Link retention to interaction strength**
Think of GLC as a race where molecules keep sticking to the stationary phase. The more strongly D sticks through intermolecular forces to the stationary phase, the slower it moves through the column, so it has the longest retention time.
Final answer: D is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase / forms stronger intermolecular forces with the stationary phase, so is retained longer.
